title: Cost-per-token is the wrong number: measured per resolved task, coding-model economics reorder — and the priciest model is almost never optimal
summary: Two independent June 2026 cost analyses converge on an insight that quietly overturns how teams pick coding models: the right unit of account is cost per resolved task, not cost per token, and switching units reshuffles the ranking. Because a weaker model retries more and burns more tokens to reach a passing patch, headline per-token price systematically mis-ranks value. Modeling a representative agentic turn at ~50k input and ~12k output tokens and dividing attempt cost by each model's SWE-bench Verified solve rate, one analysis (SSOJet, Jun 8) put DeepSeek V3.2 at ~$0.028 per resolved task versus Claude Opus 4.5 at ~$0.68 — a 24x spread for about 13 accuracy points — while Kimi K2.6 emerged as the accuracy-per-dollar sweet spot (80.2% at ~$0.075). A separate leaderboard (morphllm, Jun 28) reached the same conclusion via cost-per-benchmark-point, with Claude Haiku 4.5 leading Opus by nearly 4x on value. Academic work sharpens the point: on holistic agent leaderboards the most expensive model sits on the accuracy/cost Pareto frontier in only ~1 of 9 benchmarks, and fewer than a third of models are on the frontier at all — meaning most model choices are strictly dominated and 'buy the top of the leaderboard' is usually the wrong default. For leaders, model selection becomes a task-tiered portfolio decision keyed to cost-per-outcome and downstream risk, not a single 'best model' standard.
source: Practitioner cost leaderboards (SSOJet; morphllm), corroborated by agent-evaluation research (Holistic Agent Leaderboard / cost-of-pass)
whyItMatters: Ranking models by per-token price mis-ranks real cost: weak-but-cheap models retry more, so cost-per-resolved-task can invert the leaderboard and is the only unit that maps to money spent per unit of shipped work.
The most expensive model is on the cost/accuracy Pareto frontier in only ~1 of 9 benchmarks, so defaulting to the top-of-leaderboard model is usually paying a premium for a dominated choice.

Optimal selection is task-tiered, not global: high-volume, well-scoped work routes to cheap-but-capable models, while the accuracy points near the frontier are worth their premium mainly where a wrong patch is expensive (security-critical or hard-to-review changes).
This turns 'which model' from a standardization decision into a routing/portfolio policy that finance and engineering can jointly optimize on cost-per-outcome.
recommendedActions: Adopt cost-per-resolved-task (attempt cost ÷ solve rate) as the internal model-comparison metric instead of per-token price or raw benchmark rank.
Tier model routing by task class and risk: cheapest capable model for high-volume scoped work; frontier models reserved for hard or security-critical changes where defect cost dominates token cost.
Benchmark candidate models on your own repositories and task mix, since public solve rates and token profiles may not match your codebase.
Re-evaluate routing on a cadence — the value frontier is sparse and shifts with each model release, so today's sweet-spot model can be dominated within a cycle.
risksAndCaveats: Cost-per-resolved-task on SWE-bench is a benchmark proxy; it excludes review, rework, and integration cost, so 'resolved on benchmark' is not 'merged and correct in your repo' — real cost-per-shipped-change can differ.

The figures come from practitioner leaderboards using assumed token profiles (~50k in / ~12k out per turn) and list prices; caching, harness quality, and your actual turn counts will move the numbers.

Cheapest-per-task is not 'best': near-frontier accuracy can be worth far more than its token premium when a wrong or insecure patch is costly, so this optimizes cost, not quality, and must be balanced against risk.
